title: Working out his age at the draft
summary: A long exchange in which Albertson and Wooding try to reconcile his 1895 birth, voting at twenty, and being drafted before turning twenty-one.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: But, you must have -- well, we're talking about 1918, right? So you were twenty-three at that time, weren't you?
No, I wasn't even twenty.
When were you born?
Eighteen ninety-five.
Yeah, so you'd have to have been --
When we were drafted in 1917, and I went in in 1918, I wasn't twenty-one. And it was the draft, at that time --
But, you had to be --
Was from twenty-one to thirty-five, you see?
But, Sammy, you'd have to be if you were born in 1895.
Yeah. Now, you figure.
Yeah. And 1918, that's eighteen plus five. That's twenty-three.
No. I wasn't.
Well, how could you. Then -- there's something wrong somewhere.
I wasn't of age until -- in fact, you know how I got of age. Let's see, let's see now. Eighteen ninety-five and ten is 1905. And, that's nineteen five, isn't it?
Yeah. You're ten.
And eight would be what?
And eight? That's eighteen.
That's eighteen.
Yeah.
Well, then I'm eighteen.
No, no, no. See, 1895, okay? The year 1900, you were five years old, right?
Yeah.
So, in 1910, you were fifteen years old. In 1918, you were fifteen plus eight, you were twenty-three.
No.
You have to be.

No, I couldn't be. What, see, I'll tell you why I couldn't. When I registered, I had no right to register for the draft. Because, the reason I had no right to register for the draft was, I had been voting, from 1916 I had been voting. And posing as a man. Then, when I went up to, when I was called in the service, I wasn't, I wouldn't have turned twenty-one until I had been there five or six months.
Well, you would have to, in 1916, you'd have to be 21. Right?
Well, we registered for the draft, it was 1916.
Yeah. Well, then you were 21 years old.
Yeah, well I had to be, but I wasn't -- I hadn't turned it. I know it, for the draft, I hadn't turned quite.
Oh, I see, well when's your birthday, what month?
June.
June.
Yeah.
Um hunh.
See, I hadn't turned the year.
So you were 20. You were about to be 21.
Yeah. But I wasn't -- I had been already voting now.
Um hunh.
I can't back out of it, you know, because they'll say, well I can't register because I'm not 21.
But then, you see, by 1918, you'd have to be 23.
Well, that was. Well, I'm already registered now, in the draft, now. But, when they put the call out, I wasn't 21.
No, no. But what I'm saying is that by 1918, you were twenty-three.
Well, well.
You had to be.
Well, because, it was two years that I hadn't registered yet.
Right.
I mean I had registered, but I -- four or five months behind the time that I should have been 21.
Right.
Because from 18 to 35. That's how it happened. But, because, well, I'm in there, then so I may as well go on.
Um hunh.
I couldn't say, well I'm not of age. When I've got four or five more months. And I was anxious to go, anyhow.
Right. No, but we were talking about 1918, before, when this all came up. And you said you weren't of age yet. But you had to have been.
When I -- when I made the call, I wasn't of age. When I was drafted, I wasn't.
No, but what were we saying about 1918?
Well, that was when -- what were we saying, I don't know.
You got to Newark.
